question_text: Explore how Webster makes use of reputation in The Duchess of Malfi.
related_quotes: Marry! they are most luxurious Will wed twice
He lays down his cardinal's habit and puts on a soldier's
Whether the spirit of greatness, or of woman, Reign most in her, I know not
What can the Church force more?
I am Duchess of Malfi still
These wretched eminent things Leave no more fame behind 'em than should one Fall in a frost and leave his print in snow
Integrity of life is fame's best friend
rationale_2026: Last examined 2018 (7yr gap). Reputation/fama cluster overdue, with multiple high-leverage quotes.
content_markdown:
Webster makes use of reputation as the currency through which aristocratic power authenticates itself, and uses the play to expose that currency as systematically forged. The trajectory tracks the progressive separation of reputation from integrity: where Antonio's opening encomium imagines an ideal court in which name is grounded in virtue, the play that follows stages a court in which reputation has become detached from the conduct it purports to describe, and the only character whose reputation is consonant with her conduct — the Duchess — is destroyed in the name of an aristocratic *fama* she does not share.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster establishes reputation as the play's organising concern in Antonio's opening encomium of the French king. **[AO2]** The image of an ideal court that "Quits first his royal palace / Of flattering sycophants" and "infamous persons" establishes a normative civil-religious standard, and the image immediately afterwards of the prince's court as a "common fountain" whose poisoning spreads "death and diseases through the whole land" pathologises reputation as epidemiological: a corrupted name at the source contaminates the whole polity. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's Blackfriars audience in 1613–14 would have recognised the resonance with the Stuart court. James I's court, flooded with sycophants and rocked in 1613 by the Overbury affair — in which a courtier's reputation had been manipulated through poisoning and counter-poisoning by court favourites — had made reputation the instrument and prize of factional politics. While a generic reading sees the opening encomium as conventional Jacobean court satire, a political-historicist reading recognises Webster's stagecraft as constructing reputation as the play's covert contemporary indictment. Reputation is therefore presented as a manufactured commodity from the start.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster develops reputation as patriarchal control through the Aragonian brothers' opening interview with the Duchess. **[AO2]** Ferdinand's warning — "Marry! they are most luxurious / Will wed twice" — does not address moral conduct but reputational suspicion: a widow's remarriage was, by Jacobean dynastic convention, disapproved as compromising both family honour and inheritance. The brothers do not ask the Duchess what she has done; they instruct her in what she will be said to have done. The pre-emptive policing of reputation is dramatically significant: she has not yet endangered her *fama*, and the apparatus is mobilised against the possibility of conduct rather than the fact. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's audience would have recognised the dynamic: Jacobean disapproval of widows' remarriage operated within a dynastic political theology in which aristocratic women's conduct was understood as the family's reputational property. While a traditionalist generic reading sees the brothers' opening warning as conventional patriarchal counsel, Frank Whigham's historicist reading recovers it as status anxiety — an aristocracy compelled to police female sexuality to authenticate its own fragile nobility. Reputation is therefore presented as the operative instrument of patriarchal control over female conduct.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster develops reputation as ecclesiastical commodity through the Cardinal. **[AO2]** Antonio's account of him — that he should "have been Pope" but engineered the campaign "with money, prayers, masses" — exposes simony, but it also exposes reputation as a manufactured commodity within the post-Tridentine Catholic system. The Cardinal's opening of Act 3 — "He lays down his cardinal's habit and puts on a soldier's" — is a piece of Protestant visual polemic: reputation, the play insists, is costume. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's audience would have recognised Counter-Reformation Catholicism as the locus where ecclesiastical reputation had been most visibly debased into political instrument. While a generic reading sees the Cardinal as conventional anti-Catholic stage-villain, a more refined reading recognises Webster's stagecraft as exposing the operative divorce between conduct and name that the corrupted court systematically authenticates. Reputation is therefore presented as the surface that aristocratic power maintains in the absence of integrity.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's most refined dramatic instrument is the Duchess's relation to reputation, which Webster constructs with deliberate complexity. **[AO2]** Her secret remarriage is, on Jacobean terms, reputationally compromised: Cariola's choric aside — "Whether the spirit of greatness, or of woman, / Reign most in her, I know not; but it shows / A fearful madness" — registers, even from a sympathetic source, the reputational cost. Yet the Duchess insists, throughout, on the disjunction between conduct and name. Her invocation of *per verba de praesenti* contract — "What can the Church force more?" — argues that her conduct is honourable even if her *fama* will be impugned. Her great line "I am Duchess of Malfi still", uttered to Bosola in the torture chamber at 4.2, asserts that reputation is grounded in identity rather than in what is said about it. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's audience would have recognised the *Ars Moriendi* tradition's requirement that the dying compose a final reputation through their conduct on the deathbed, and Webster's careful staging of her death is a textbook execution of dying well. While a traditionalist reading sees her marriage as transgressive of social order, a feminist reading recognises Webster's stagecraft as converting her reputation, in Jacobean terms, from compromised widow to martyr.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's most ambivalent witness to reputation is Bosola. **[AO2]** His opening complaint that he has been rewarded only with "the wages of sin" registers the malcontent figure's grievance that his reputation as a spy and instrument has displaced his earlier identity as scholar-soldier. Yet his very ambivalence makes him the play's most penetrating diagnostician of reputation: it is Bosola who delivers the great memento mori meditations to the Duchess in Act 4. His disguise as the bell-man, with the dirge "Hark, now everything is still", weaponises the funeral genre that ratifies reputation in death. After the murder he is ravaged by recognition that he has destroyed an integrity his masters lacked: "These wretched eminent things / Leave no more fame behind 'em than should one / Fall in a frost and leave his print in snow" — a sententia that converts the brothers' aristocratic *fama* into a melting trace. While a traditionalist reading sees Bosola's conversion as conventional revenge tragedy belated recognition, a more refined reading recognises Webster's stagecraft as positioning him as the dramatic instrument through which the reputation-discourse of the corrupted court is finally exposed.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's closing dramatic operation exposes the bankruptcy of reputational discourse. **[AO2]** Antonio dies by accident, killed by Bosola in mistaken identity for the Cardinal, in violence so poorly motivated that no reputational meaning can be extracted from it. The Cardinal's death, achieved by his own henchmen, is presided over by the courtiers who refuse to enter — their feigned indifference an icy parody of the *fama* he had cultivated. The closing sententia — "Integrity of life is fame's best friend" — appears to restore the normative order of Antonio's opening encomium, but it does so in the wreckage of every character whose conduct could have ratified it. While a traditionalist generic reading sees the closing sententia as conventional Jacobean moral restoration, a more sceptical reading recognises Webster's stagecraft as exposing reputation as the most untrustworthy of the court's instruments: a *fama* manufactured in the absence of integrity, surviving its bearers no longer than a footprint in melting snow.

**[Conclusion linked to question]** Webster therefore makes use of reputation as the dramatic instrument through which the corrupted court is anatomised at its operative foundation. The opening pathologised image of the fountain, the Aragonian brothers' pre-emptive policing, the Cardinal's manufactured ecclesiastical *fama*, the Duchess's integrity that grounds reputation in identity, Bosola's late recognition of reputation as melting trace, and the closing sententia delivered amid the wreckage of every character who could have authenticated it together constitute the play's dramatic anatomy of reputation in Jacobean political theology. Reputation is presented as the surface that aristocratic power maintains in the absence of integrity, and the play's most exact judgement is that, when integrity is absent, reputation cannot survive its bearer no longer than a footprint in melting snow.
